transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2026-12-12 14:00 UTC
- Duration: 54 mins
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Samir (CTO, Oxbridge), Elena (Lead ML Eng), Marcus (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, I'm the account lead for Oxbridge. Maya will drive the tech walkthrough. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:12] Samir: Yep, hearing you. Thanks for setting this up. We're curious about the migration story — we're running a mix of OpenAI and some Together endpoints right now.
[00:22] Maya: Great, cool. Today I want to show two things: parity mapping from typical OpenAI/Together calls to the Redwood API, and a quick tour of the Console + Optimize suggestions for cost/latency. We'll also cover private deployment constraints since I know you have VPC requirements.
[00:38] Elena: Awesome. We have a pretty complex prompt set, lots of function-calling flows and streaming for our chat UI. We also use KV caching patterns in some places, and we need to preserve that.
[00:49] Jordan: Noted. Can you describe current volumes and SLOs?
[00:52] Samir: Baseline is around 350 QPS daytime, spikes up to 1.8k during batch windows. Latency SLO for interactive features is 200-250ms tail, cost target is effectively half of our current per-token spend if possible.
[01:12] Marcus: Also, we need audit logs stored for 13 months and everything has to go through our KMS; SOC2 compliance is a must.
[01:20] Maya: Ok good. On the parity piece — a couple of common gotchas: function calling maps pretty directly to Redwood's structured outputs; streaming and chunked responses are supported via our streaming endpoint. The biggest differences you'll hit are around model naming and some default decoding params.
[01:40] Elena: When you say model naming, is that just renames or are there behavior changes?
[01:44] Maya: Mostly names and a few default tokenization/temperature defaults. For example, what you're calling gpt-4x in your stack might correspond to redwood/g4x-v1 or a quantized variant; we provide mapping guidance and our Optimize tool will recommend quantization profiles if you need cost savings.
[02:02] Samir: How do you handle KV cache for chat? We currently keep long context and rely on prefix cache to keep costs down.
[02:08] Maya: Redwood supports KV cache persistence and prefix caching; sometimes transcriptions show it as "K V cash" in our older notes, haha. You can pin conversation state to a cache key and we do automatic eviction based on policy. Our runtime can serve warmed caches to reduce token decode.
[02:25] Jordan: For the migration path: most customers do a staged endpoint swap — keep original endpoints live, route a percent of traffic to Redwood for parity checks, run regressions with your eval set, then ramp. The Console has rollouts and automatic fallback rules if latency or quality regresses.
[02:44] Elena: Is that the same for Together models? We use a mixture.
[02:47] Maya: Yes, same idea. Together and Anthropic mappings are similar; the main work is prompt tuning and decoding param adjustments. We provide a parity spreadsheet with suggested prompt deltas and decoding configs.
[02:59] Samir: What about streaming? We rely on streaming for lower perceived latency on desktop clients.
[03:04] Maya: Our streaming uses chunked transfer and supports delta updates. One thing to watch — some client libraries expect a different end-of-stream marker; we document that. There's also the function-calling interleaving caveat where chunking + function calls need careful mapping, but we have example code in the docs.
[03:25] Marcus: Network-wise, we can't have outbound egress to arbitrary IPs from our VPC; we need either a private peering or a dedicated private deployment. What are our options?
[03:34] Jordan: Two main options: Redwood Hosted with VPC peering (private egress + dedicated capacity pools) or Redwood Private (customer VPC/on-prem package). Hosted VPC peering is faster to start, Private is for stricter data control. Both integrate with KMS/HSM for key management.
[03:51] Marcus: Latency-wise, are you seeing sub-200ms tails for 2k QPS on dedicated pools?
[03:57] Maya: Depends on model size and batching. For smaller models with aggressive batching and low-latency kernels we see sub-150ms median and low 99s in dedicated configs. For the larger 8k-token contexts it's more expensive and higher tails. Optimize can recommend batching and quantization to hit cost/latency tradeoffs.
[04:18] Elena: About quantization — do you have benchmarks comparing int8 vs int4 tradeoffs for our use case? We worry about quality regressions.
[04:25] Maya: We do. Our Optimize tooling will run a paired eval — you'll get quality regression scores against your eval prompts. We usually recommend a canary with quantized variant and run A/B against baseline for a week.
[04:38] Samir: Security: SOC2 report, ISO, SSO integrations — can you supply those docs?
[04:44] Jordan: Yes, we'll send SOC2 Type II, ISO certs, and our SAML SSO configuration docs. We'll also provide details on audit log retention and how to ship logs to your SIEM.
[04:56] Marcus: For the audit logs, can we push via syslog/S3 to our account?
[05:00] Maya: Yes, you can export logs to a customer-owned S3 or stream to syslog/CloudWatch. For Private deployments you retain everything in your tenancy.
[05:10] Jordan: Quick console tour — Maya?
[05:12] Maya: Sure. (screen share) First, model catalog: you can see Redwood-verified performance profiles. Here we can pin a model version to a route, attach rollout policy — canary percentages, time windows, auto-fallback. There's a tracing pane that ties token-level latency back to CPU/GPU traces.
[05:34] Elena: Can we set a token-level cost cap per route?
[05:38] Maya: Yes, there's token budget enforcement per API key/route. You can also set token-based alerts and quota-based throttles.
[05:45] Marcus: In the runtime traces do you show batch sizes and kernel choice?
[05:49] Maya: We show batch distributions, observed kernel, and a recommended kernel selection for the observed pattern. Sometimes the telemetry mislabels kernel names in raw exports but it's in the UI.
[06:00] [Speaker 1]: (inaudible)
[06:03] Maya: Back to parity mapping, here's an example mapping for a simple chat completion call. OpenAI sample: createChatCompletion(model=gpt-4o, messages=[...], stream=true, function_call="auto"). Redwood equivalent is a fairly thin swap: POST /v1/generate with model redwood/g4o-v1, body= {..} and stream=true. The code diff is usually 5-15 lines. There are a couple of places where you may need to tweak stop sequences and system role handling.
[06:36] Elena: We have several legacy helpers that rely on OpenAI SDK behaviors; how much rewrite is typically needed?
[06:42] Maya: Minimal in most cases. We provide client libraries that mimic OpenAI shape for common languages; for complex bindings you might adapt the glue code.
[06:51] Samir: Any pitfalls with token accounting? Our billing ties to per-token and we're sensitive to mismatch when swapping providers.
[06:57] Jordan: Tokenization differences can cause 5-15% delta. We include a tokenization mapping report and a tokenization equivalence tool so you can run your corpus and see token deltas before switching. That should help forecast cost.
[07:14] Marcus: What about rate limiting? We saw throttles in our previous vendor during spikes.
[07:19] Maya: We offer per-key quotas and adaptive burst capacity. For Dedicated you can buy reserved capacity with guaranteed throughput. There's also a fallback policy so if a route exceeds the SLO we can shift traffic to a cheaper compatible variant to maintain availability.
[07:34] Elena: Can we test function calling behavior with our own functions?
[07:37] Maya: Yes, we support schema-based function calling and you can pass your OpenAPI-like function schemas; the output comes back in the same structure. There are some quirks around nested JSON and streaming; we show examples in the parity sheet.
[07:52] Samir: Let's talk about the evaluation step you mentioned — how do you typically run regressions?
[07:56] Jordan: Customers provide a sanitized prompt/test set, we run paired comparisons across models and variants, then provide quality/regression metrics plus token-cost breakdown. We can run this in your account or on a Redwood sandbox.
[08:09] Elena: Would you mind demonstrating a small eval run real quick with one of our sample prompts?
[08:13] Maya: Sure, if you paste one sample we can demo a quick compare between current provider output and a Redwood mapped model.
[08:21] [08:21] Elena (screen): Paste sample prompt: "Summarize the patient's recent lab results and highlight potential drug interactions."
[08:28] Maya: Running a quick paired compare... (typing) Okay, here's the output from your current vendor and here's Redwood g4o-v1 output. You can see slight differences in punctuation and some hallucination tangents we flagged. Our eval shows a 0.7% regression on the Rouge-like metric for that prompt set, but when we applied a small prompt delta and temperature tweak it closed to parity.
[08:58] Samir: Good to see the delta. Can you share that parity spreadsheet?
[09:02] Jordan: Yes, we'll send it after the call with specific recommended prompt diffs and decoding settings.
[09:08] Marcus: Network/peering next steps — checklist for our infra team?
[09:12] Jordan: We'll send a short checklist: required CIDR ranges, TLS cert requirements, optional peering vs public egress, and SAML config endpoints.
[09:21] Elena: For bench runs, are you running on our data or synthetic? We prefer synthetic + sampled real prompts to avoid PHI leakage.
[09:28] Maya: Totally — we recommend sanitized samples. We can also run in an isolated sandbox if you want extra separation.
[09:35] Samir: Pricing — high level — do you have estimator tooling?
[09:39] Jordan: Yes, our cost estimator takes tokenization deltas and estimated QPS to provide TCO comparisons across hosted, dedicated, and private deploys. We'll attach an initial estimate in the spreadsheet.
[09:52] Elena: Any gotchas on function call streaming and large responses? We sometimes hit timeouts when functions stream multiple chunks.
[09:59] Maya: For that pattern we recommend chunked streaming with early function invocation and progressive flush. We also have a server-side TTL to avoid client timeouts. We'll include an example.
[10:13] Marcus: For SSO and RBAC, can we map Redwood roles to our internal groups?
[10:17] Jordan: Yes SAML mappings, SCIM provisioning for users, and RBAC roles that map to your groups. You can also lock down per-route keys.
[10:25] Samir: Ok, looks good. What would a pilot look like?
[10:28] Jordan: Pilot often runs 2-4 weeks: ingest sanitized prompt set, run parity mapping + small A/B traffic (5-10%), measure latency/quality, then iterate on prompt deltas and quantization. After success you pick a ramp schedule.
[10:42] Elena: Any downtime risk during cutover?
[10:45] Maya: Very low if you use staged rollouts and fallback policies. We can also do a shadow mode to collect telemetry without returning Redwood outputs to users.
[10:55] Samir: Good. One more on data residency — our EU customers require data to stay in EU. You support region pinning?
[11:01] Jordan: Yes, you can pin routes to EU regions and for Private we'll deploy in your selected region.
[11:08] Marcus: Ok we'll need the VPC checklist and the parity sheet. Also please include an example bench harness we can run internally.
[11:15] Jordan: Will do. Maya, anything else to show?
[11:17] Maya: Quick final note on Optimize: it surfaces batching thresholds, cache hit targets, and quantization profiles. It also suggests model variants for a given latency budget; we can auto-generate a suggested config you can import into the Console.
[11:33] Elena: That import feature — does it preserve rollout config?
[11:36] Maya: It does, and you can tweak percentages before applying.
[11:39] [11:39] Samir: Ok let's recap next steps.
[11:41] Jordan: Recap: Jordan sends parity spreadsheet + pricing + SOC2/ISO + VPC checklist; Maya runs bench and shares results; Oxbridge to send sanitized prompts and network diagram. We'll aim to touch base after bench results.
[11:58] Samir: Sounds good, thanks both.
[12:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcript.
